newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tells Russian government to prove itself.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tells Russian government to prove itself.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin told Russia's new government on Tuesday it must prove itself by making a breakthrough to end chronic wage delays and improve tax collection.

Yeltsin, trying to put Russia's house in order and reassert his authority after a long absence through illness, also told parliament to improve its work and signed a decree intended to step up the fight against corruption.
His demands had a familiar ring and again highlighted the Russian leadership's long-term failure to solve the problems as much as a new will to tackle them.

"In the president's opinion, the situation with wages and pensions remains difficult," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters after Yeltsin's weekly meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

"The president thinks it is necessary to finally achieve a breakthrough to demonstrate the government's ability to meet its obligations. Looking at tax collection, the president told the government to act decisively."
Yastrzhembsky gave few details of the decree "On Priority Measures to Prevent Corruption and Reduce Budgetary Spending in Organising the Purchases for State Needs".

But he said it was intended to ensure effective use of the state budget and to prevent abuses by civil servants making official purchases and orders, a scourge that has defied efforts to wipe it out since tsarist times.
Yeltsin, 66, told Chernomyrdin to prepare a report with guidelines for Russia's 1998 budget by April 20 and to speed up a long-awaited new tax code.
Chernomyrdin, who turns 59 on Wednesday, is a long-term ally of the president and has kept his job in a government reshuffle that has gradually unfolded in the past few weeks.

But Yeltsin says the previous government, under Chernomyrdin's command, failed to push through economic changes and he has brought in two young reform-minded first deputy prime ministers to oversee the reforms.

Delays of several months in payment of wages and pensions prompted a day of nationwide protests last month which failed to attract as much support as trade unions had hoped but signalled that workers' patience is not endless.
Chernomyrdin has attributed the government's inability to pay wages and pensions mainly to widespread tax evasion.
The tax collection crisis has forced the government and parliamentary officials to consider changes in the 1997 budget to cut spending for the remainder of the year.
But communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, whose party is the largest group in the State Duma lower house of parliament, said his party would oppose such moves.
"Instead of revitalising industry and conducting a normal tax policy, ministers are keeping the old fiscal policy...and here they will go bankrupt and break their necks," he said.

Yeltsin said at the end of February, when he was returning from months of heart trouble and pneumonia, that he would take on the parliament if it picked a fight, reviving memories of how he dissolved the previous parliament in 1993 and then used tanks to crush a rebellion by hardline parliamentarians.
Such a confrontation is unlikely now, but Yeltsin expressed his dissatisfaction with the Duma's work during talks with its chairman, Gennady Seleznyov.
Yeltsin said he had recently been forced to return three out of every four legislative acts approved by the Duma because they were poorly prepared.
